unsolicitedOpinions.shortTitle: Boxes and tables deserve art direction
unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: A well-styled table is a paper's second face. Over the years I've built a small design system of boxes and tables—and, flatteringly, colleagues and students have started to copy it.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
I care, probably too much, about how tables and boxes render in a paper. Over the years I've converged on a small set of styles I reuse across my work, and I've had the quiet pleasure of seeing several colleagues and PhD students adopt them in their own papers. It happens every few months: I open a draft or a reading list, I spot one of my boxes living its best life in someone else's submission, and my day is made. I always make a point of thanking them.

A small ask

If you end up using any of these, a brief mention in the acknowledgements of your paper would mean a lot. I'm planning, at some point, a little literature review to see how quietly these have spread—so the acknowledgement also helps me not miss you. And a screenshot still makes my week, always.

Below are the ones I actually use. My preambles contain a small graveyard of experimental variants I tried and dropped—I'll spare you those. For each box, you'll see the LaTeX code on the left and two previews on the right: the box on its own, and the way I actually decorate it in my papers—with a small FontAwesome icon next to the label. A bullseye or a question mark before a research question, a bar chart before a summary. It's a habit more than a rule, but it gives a paper a consistent visual grammar across sections.

Required packages

All the definitions below lean on a handful of LaTeX packages. Drop these into your preamble before the definitions and you're set:

% Boxes and icons
\usepackage{xcolor}                  % for gray!15 tints
\usepackage{mdframed}                % stebox* styles (boxes 1 and 3)
\usepackage[breakable]{tcolorbox}    % rqboxC and rqsummary (boxes 2 and 4)
\usepackage{fontawesome}             % \faBullseye, \faQuestionCircle, \faBarChart

% Tables
\usepackage{booktabs}                % \toprule, \midrule, \bottomrule
\usepackage{threeparttable}          % caption + table + notes as one unit
1. Left-accent RQ box

Based on mdframed with a single thin left rule and a light-gray fill. Quiet, inline-friendly. I use it to quote a research question next to the paragraph that introduces it.

\mdfdefinestyle{stebox5}{%
  linecolor=black, linewidth=1pt,
  leftmargin=0cm, rightmargin=0cm,
  roundcorner=5pt,
  topline=false, bottomline=false,
  rightline=false, leftline=true,
  backgroundcolor=gray!15
}

\newcommand{\steResearchQuestionBox}[1]{%
  \begin{mdframed}[style=stebox5]
    #1
  \end{mdframed}
}

% ---- Usage ----
% Plain
\steResearchQuestionBox{%
  \textbf{RQ}---\textit{What individual factors influence
  developers' choices to use LLMs for specific SE purposes?}
}

% With icon
\steResearchQuestionBox{%
  \faBullseye\ \textbf{RQ}---\textit{What individual factors
  influence developers' choices to use LLMs for specific SE purposes?}
}
Plain

RQ—What individual factors influence developers' choices to use LLMs for specific SE purposes?

With icon

RQ—What individual factors influence developers' choices to use LLMs for specific SE purposes?

2. Self-contained RQ pull-out

Same idea but with a full thin border instead of a single left rule. Heavier presence—useful when the RQ is the visual anchor of the subsection rather than a sidebar.

\newtcolorbox{rqboxC}{
  colback=gray!10,
  colframe=black,
  boxrule=0.4pt,
  left=6pt, right=6pt,
  top=4pt, bottom=4pt,
  breakable
}

% ---- Usage ----
% Plain
\begin{rqboxC}
  \textbf{RQ1}---Which DoI antecedents predict the use of QSTs
  across the three functional clusters?
\end{rqboxC}

% With icon
\begin{rqboxC}
  \faQuestionCircle\ \textbf{RQ1}---Which DoI antecedents predict
  the use of QSTs across the three functional clusters?
\end{rqboxC}
Plain

RQ1—Which DoI antecedents predict the use of QSTs across the three functional clusters?

With icon

RQ1—Which DoI antecedents predict the use of QSTs across the three functional clusters?

3. Summary-of-results box

Horizontal rules top and bottom, titled header in bold, light-gray body. I put this at the end of every RQ subsection as a tl;dr of the finding.

\mdfdefinestyle{steboxSummaryWhite}{%
  linecolor=black, linewidth=1pt,
  leftmargin=0cm, rightmargin=0cm,
  roundcorner=5pt,
  topline=true, bottomline=true,
  rightline=false, leftline=false,
  backgroundcolor=gray!15,
  frametitlebackgroundcolor=white,
  frametitlerule=true,
  frametitlerulewidth=1pt
}

\newcommand{\steSummaryBox}[2]{%
  \begin{mdframed}[style=steboxSummaryWhite,
                   frametitle={\textbf{#1}}]
    #2
  \end{mdframed}
}

% ---- Usage ----
% Plain
\steSummaryBox{Summary of the Results.}{%
  The analysis confirms that the model is reliable and
  well-suited for predicting the dependent variables.
  Habit emerges as a strong predictor.
}

% With icon
\steSummaryBox{\faBarChart\ Summary of the Results.}{%
  The analysis confirms that the model is reliable and
  well-suited for predicting the dependent variables.
  Habit emerges as a strong predictor.
}
Plain
Summary of the Results.
The analysis confirms that the model is reliable and well-suited for predicting the dependent variables. Habit emerges as a strong predictor, reinforcing the notion that adoption is context-dependent rather than uniform.
With icon
Summary of the Results.
The analysis confirms that the model is reliable and well-suited for predicting the dependent variables. Habit emerges as a strong predictor, reinforcing the notion that adoption is context-dependent rather than uniform.
4. Dark-titled RQ + answer card

A black bar on top with the question in white, a light body below with the answer. The clearest signal I've found for “this is what we found, you can stop reading now if you want.” I use one per RQ in the Results.

\newtcolorbox{rqsummary}[1]{%
  title={#1},
  coltitle=white,
  fonttitle=\small\bfseries,
  colbacktitle=black!85,
  colback=gray!10,
  colframe=black!85,
  boxrule=0.4pt,
  left=6pt, right=6pt,
  top=4pt, bottom=4pt,
  toptitle=3pt, bottomtitle=3pt,
  arc=3pt, outer arc=3pt,
  breakable
}

% ---- Usage ----
% Plain
\begin{rqsummary}{RQ1---Which DoI antecedents predict the use
of QSTs across the three functional clusters?}
  DoI attributes explain QST use at the functional-cluster
  level, but unevenly. Relative advantage yields the largest
  coefficients; ease of use is significant across all three
  composites.
\end{rqsummary}

% With icon
\begin{rqsummary}{\faQuestionCircle\ RQ1---Which DoI
antecedents predict the use of QSTs across the three
functional clusters?}
  DoI attributes explain QST use at the functional-cluster
  level, but unevenly. Relative advantage yields the largest
  coefficients; ease of use is significant across all three
  composites.
\end{rqsummary}
Plain
RQ1—Which DoI antecedents predict the use of QSTs across the three functional clusters?
DoI attributes explain QST use at the functional-cluster level, but unevenly. Relative advantage yields the largest coefficients; ease of use is the only antecedent significant across all three composites. Other effects are cluster-specific.
With icon
RQ1—Which DoI antecedents predict the use of QSTs across the three functional clusters?
DoI attributes explain QST use at the functional-cluster level, but unevenly. Relative advantage yields the largest coefficients; ease of use is the only antecedent significant across all three composites. Other effects are cluster-specific.
5. Table pattern

Not a custom environment, but a consistent assembly: threeparttable so footnotes sit with the table; booktabs rules (\toprule, \midrule, \bottomrule—no vertical lines, heavier top/bottom, thin midrule); @{} at both ends of the tabular spec to kill the default outer column padding; and a tablenotes block for any caveat. Always \small, always flushleft notes.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\begin{threeparttable}
\caption{Reliability and Convergent Validity.}
\label{tab:reliability}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Construct} & $\alpha$ & $\rho_c$ & AVE \\
\midrule
Relative Advantage (RA) & .894 & .914 & .543 \\
Ease of Use (EoU)\tnote{a} & .794 & .879 & .708 \\
Observability (Obs) & .758 & .846 & .584 \\
Compatibility (Com) & .803 & .884 & .718 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\begin{tablenotes}[flushleft]\footnotesize
\item[a] EoU3 dropped (outer loading = .151).
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}

unsolicitedOpinions.shortTitle: The em dash is the king of punctuation
unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: Hyphen, en dash, em dash: three different characters, three different jobs. Most people only know one of them.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
There are (at least) three horizontal lines you can type, and they are not interchangeable:

  • Hyphen (-): glues words together. state-of-the-art, well-known.
  • En dash (–): ranges and connections. pages 12–18, the Rome–Naples train.
  • Em dash (—): interrupts a sentence—like this—with more force than a comma and less than parentheses.

I am a devout em-dash user. It is elegant, expressive, and—crucially for anyone writing proposals with a hard character limit—I use the canonical form without spaces around it, which saves two characters every single time. Small victories.

If you take nothing else from this rant: please stop typing a hyphen when you mean an em dash. Your sentences deserve better.

postscript.title: P.S.—plot twist
postscript.body:
LLMs, it turns out, have a notable fondness for the em dash. So much so that AI-detection tools now treat heavy em-dash use as circumstantial evidence of AI-generated text. Out of curiosity, I ran a few of my own pre-LLM papers through one of these detectors—and several came back flagged as “likely AI-written,” for no reason other than my decade-long, pre-existing love affair with the character.

It's a small tragedy: a perfectly good piece of punctuation being recast as a smoking gun for a crime it had no part in. We should resist. Keep writing em dashes. Defend the em dash.

unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: The superscript number belongs after the comma or period, not before it. Yes, even in that paper you're reading right now.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
In English-language style guides (Chicago, APA, MLA, and essentially every major publisher), footnote and endnote markers are placed after the punctuation they follow, not before:

Wrong: …a well-established result3.
Right: …a well-established result.3

And yet, you will find this error in a surprising number of published papers—including, occasionally, in venues that really should know better. It's not a matter of life and death, but it is a small, satisfying signal that the authors (or the typesetters) care about the details.

Caveat: French typographic convention places the marker before the punctuation, so if you are writing in French you get a free pass. Everyone else: after the comma, after the period, always.

unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: A paragraph is a unit of thought, not a visual break. One idea per paragraph—and the sequence should tell a story.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
A paragraph is not a visual break to rest the reader's eyes; it is a unit of thought. It introduces one idea, develops it, and wraps it up—one paragraph, one concept. If yours is trying to cover three, it's three paragraphs in a trench coat.

Beyond the single paragraph there's the question of sequence. The paragraphs in a section should read like short chapters of a story: each picks up where the previous one left off, and together they build an argument. A useful test: read only the first sentence of each paragraph in order—does it give you a coherent outline of what the section is arguing? If not, the paragraphs are misorganised, no matter how polished each one is in isolation.

In LaTeX specifically: a paragraph break is a blank line in the source. Not \\, not \newline—those do something else entirely and will usually break your layout. The blank line is the canonical marker; LaTeX takes care of indentation and vertical spacing based on the document class. Many students discover this much later than they should.

The failure mode I see most often in drafts: a paragraph gets broken because the previous one “looked long enough.” That's formatting as aesthetics rather than as argument. Before breaking, ask yourself: does the next paragraph actually introduce a new concept, or am I just catching my breath? If the latter, don't break.

unsolicitedOpinions.shortTitle: ISO 8601 is the only correct date format
unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: YYYY-MM-DD. It sorts lexicographically, it's unambiguous across continents, and it never asks whether 03/04/2026 is March or April.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
Is 03/04/2026 the 3rd of April or the 4th of March? Depends which side of the Atlantic you're on. Is 2026-04-03 ambiguous? No. It is the 3rd of April, 2026, and it will still be the 3rd of April, 2026 if you email it to someone in Tokyo, Palo Alto, or Salerno.

The ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD) has a stack of quiet superpowers:

  • It is globally unambiguous. There is exactly one interpretation.
  • It sorts correctly as a plain string. ls, spreadsheets, and filenames all agree on the order.
  • It plays nicely with timestamps: append T and you're already most of the way to a full datetime.

This is the hill. File names, folder names, changelogs, commit messages, shopping lists, archaeological records of my own life—all ISO 8601. If you catch me writing 04/19/26, assume I have been replaced by an impostor.

unsolicitedOpinions.shortTitle: Titan is the most interesting place in the solar system
unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: Saturn's largest moon has methane seas, methane rain, and maybe methane-based life. The most dynamic place we've ever found—and nobody talks about it.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
Credit where due

Everything below I learned from my cousin Alfonso Cavallo, the family's unofficial Titan evangelist for as long as I can remember. I'm just the megaphone with a website.

I won't keep you long. Titan is the single most interesting place in the solar system and almost nobody talks about it. Let me try to change that.

The basics. Titan is Saturn's largest moon, and it is bigger than the planet Mercury—planet-sized, just orbiting the wrong star. It has a thick orange-hazy atmosphere (roughly 1.45× Earth's surface pressure), made mostly of nitrogen with a generous serving of methane. In principle, you could strap wings to your arms and fly around, if you could breathe nitrogen-methane and survive a bracing -179°C ambient.

The methane cycle. Here's where it gets good. Titan is the only other body in the solar system with a complete hydrological cycle—except the “water” is liquid methane and ethane. It evaporates from surface seas, forms clouds, rains back down, and carves rivers, deltas, and canyons into the terrain. Three enormous polar seas—Kraken Mare, Ligeia Mare, and Punga Mare—plus a network of river channels. The Cassini spacecraft (in orbit around Saturn from 2004 to 2017) actually mapped the coastlines with radar. An entire weather system using a solvent that's a gas on Earth.

The seas move. Shorelines shift with the seasons—and each Titan season lasts about seven Earth years, so dynamics play out slowly but visibly across a mission lifetime. Cassini caught magic islands: bright patches on the sea surface that appear and then vanish between flybys. Probably nitrogen bubbles, floating solids, or foam from waves. Nobody has nailed it down. And yes, there are tides, because Saturn is a gravitationally heavy neighbour and the seas respond.

The weird part. There's a small astrobiology thread that hypothesises methane-based life: organisms using liquid methane as a solvent the way Earth life uses water, consuming hydrogen and acetylene, producing methane. Cassini observed a hydrogen flux that seems to disappear near the surface—which could be consistent with such a metabolism, or could just be surface chemistry doing something boring. Nobody knows yet. NASA's Dragonfly mission—a nuclear-powered rotorcraft, launching in 2028 and arriving in 2034—is designed to land there and look harder.

If the solar system were a dinner party, Mars is the self-important one who keeps talking about colonisation, Europa and Enceladus are the mysterious types everyone has a crush on, and Titan is the one in the corner with a complete alien chemistry ecosystem and methane rain, quietly being the most interesting creature in the room.

unsolicitedOpinions.shortTitle: I am the best gamer in the department
unsolicitedOpinions.hotTake: There is a sign on my office door that says so. Exhibit A: I finished Dark Souls blindfolded, on stream, and the VODs are still out there if you know where to look.
unsolicitedOpinions.body:
There is a sign on my office door. It reads, more or less: Best gamer in the department. It's half a joke and half—I now claim—an empirical fact, with witnesses and timestamps.

The evidence: I finished Dark Souls from start to credits blindfolded. The run was streamed live; the VODs are still floating around the internet for anyone curious enough to look. I'm not linking them—part of the charm is that you have to go find the proof yourself.

How it works. Less impressive than it sounds, more impressive than it has any right to be. The setup: I held the controller, blindfolded; someone next to me called out the room—where the character was standing, what was ahead, what was off to the side. The game took care of the rest. Dark Souls has, almost as a side effect of being a good game, an unusually generous audio layer: every enemy has a distinct breath, footstep, and weapon swing; rooms echo differently; even the menus have an audible cursor. A patient voice in your ear, plus the audio, plus enough deaths to learn the geometry—it adds up to a playable game.

The hard parts aren't the ones you'd guess. Bosses turn into metronomes: tell, attack, roll, repeat. The mean parts are the corridors and the ledges—the geometry, not the enemies. There was a lot of falling. There was, eventually, no falling.

So: best gamer in the department. The sign stays up. If a colleague wishes to dispute the claim, I am happy to accept under the same conditions, with the same blindfold, on a game of their choosing—peer review by combat.
